description: sound-angels is a Dark Room-like browser game where music is combat: text, buttons, and step grids rendered as DOM elements. Start with README.md for the concept, stack (Vite, React, Tailwind, Zustand, Tone.js), and save format, then read docs/mechanics.md for the core design — the ATB battle system, chord progressions, loop-station melody recording, party positions, and enemy variants. These two documents are the roadmap for everything that follows.
title: Project Overview

description: The browser shell in index.html mounts the React app at #root and loads src/main.tsx, which mounts the App component inside StrictMode. App.tsx wires global keyboard input, reads phase state from the session store, and routes between menu, prep, combat, and result overlays. This thin entry layer owns no game rules — it only boots React and hands control to the engine and screens below.
title: Application Entry Point

description: Building on the design docs, the vendored zero-dependency theory core in theory.ts defines scale degrees, Roman-numeral chord voicings, and progression scoring — it is one of the most depended-upon modules in the project. keys.ts sits beside it with the playable combat-key pool plus random selection and scripted overrides. Together they form the musical vocabulary: every chord, melody, and fight key elsewhere resolves through these tables.
languageLesson: TypeScript zero-dependency modules like theory.ts use plain lookup tables and pure functions so the engine stays serializable and testable — no classes, no side effects, deterministic output for a given input.
title: Music Theory Foundation

description: The arrangement model stores music as data: melody tracks and drum grids plus Roman-numeral chords, deliberately keeping scale degrees and numerals rather than absolute pitches until the audio boundary. melodyBank.ts provides three factory preset templates for pre-fight preparation, while presets.ts adds combat melody-set presets with content-hash dedupe, tombstoned deletes, and tick-based cooldowns. Editing the loop here is what the player actually does to fight — notes are attacks.
title: Loop Arrangement Model

description: The combat engine advances one 16th-step tick at a time, resolving melody damage, chord blessings, enemy ATB gauges, and parry/QTE charts — it has the broadest scope in the codebase because it reads the arrangement, theory, data, and chart modules. units.ts provides the shared fighter model for party and foes with shield-first damage, healing, and tick-based buffs. Combat state stays pure TypeScript and JSON-serializable, with no Tone.js, React, or DOM inside.
title: Combat Tick Engine

description: Skill expression during fights comes from the pure QTE chart model in qte.ts — tap/hold notes, melody and harmonic chart builders, and press/release scoring with parry damage scaling. parryChart.ts generates seeded ZXCV tap-and-hold motifs shaped by per-enemy pattern parameters, so charts stay deterministic under test. perform.ts adds the WASD relative-motion performance cursor with ZXCV parry keys and step/millisecond tempo helpers used by both engine timing and the UI playhead.
title: QTE and Parry Charts

description: The session singleton holds arrangement and fight state outside React and exposes a subscribe mirror for the UI, keeping rules in the engine and rendering in React. phase.ts defines the menu/prep/combat/victory/defeat state machine with transition validation, while positions.ts maps party members to chord, beat, and front slots (front-row lanes double as melody lanes). session.ts ties it together: selecting encounters, locking the fight key at fight creation, reconciling potency and cooldowns, and routing QTE input.
title: Session State Hub

description: Static balance and content live outside the engine so tuning never touches combat logic. enemies.ts defines enemy profiles with stats, weaknesses, and serializable timbre recipes consumed by both combat and audio, while encounters.ts curates multi-enemy templates of escalating difficulty with linear unlock helpers. roster.ts names the playable characters with instruments and roles, and chords.ts pairs chord-progression presets with tier-gated combat blessings derived from progression scores.
title: Game Data and Balance

description: The browser-only Tone.js renderer reads engine snapshots and never writes combat state. context.ts owns AudioContext startup and the shared master gain/limiter bus, started only on explicit user gesture, while synths.ts allocates the pooled voice bank once (per-instrument leads, pads, bass, shared drums) instead of constructing synths per note. player.ts bridges the two worlds, rendering arrangement snapshots into drum, bass, melody-lane, and chord-pad voices on every 16th step via the Transport.
languageLesson: Tone.js voices are expensive to construct, so synths.ts pools them once at startup and reuses them per step. AudioContext autoplay policies require a user gesture, which is why playback is gated behind ensureAudio in context.ts.
title: Audio Rendering Layer

description: React never touches the engine directly — useSessionStore.ts is a thin Zustand mirror subscribed to the session singleton, wiring arrangement, combat, audio player, and WASD performance actions into components. storage.ts provides guarded localStorage helpers persisting cleared encounters, selected party, custom chords, and tutorial state across reloads. This bridge is the only sanctioned path between the pure engine and the presentation layer.
languageLesson: Zustand stores subscribe to external sources via a subscribe function, mirroring engine state into React without letting components mutate it. Guarded localStorage access (try/catch, schema checks) keeps saves robust against corrupt or missing data.
title: State Bridge and Saves

description: The Dark Room-style flow becomes visible here: PrepScreen is the battle-preparation workstation for key and tempo tuning, chord progression, melody bank, loop sequencer, and party formation, while CombatScreen composes the foe panel, step grid, QTE panel, party cards, and combat log with halt/retreat control. StepGrid is the main step-sequencer editor for melody lanes, per-bar chords, performer slots, and drum rows, and QtePanel renders the always-visible chart highway driven by the audio-clock-anchored playhead. Every widget reads the Zustand mirror and sends edits back through the session.
title: Screens and Sequencer UI

description: The package manifest declares the dev/build/test/lint scripts and runtime dependencies (React, Tone.js, Zustand) plus Vitest, while vite.config.ts wires the build with the @/* to src/* alias and the test setup. Typecheck runs first via tsc -b in the build script, oxlint handles linting, and Vitest covers the engine with seeded RNG — never importing Tone.js in src/game. Knowing these two files tells you how to run, verify, and extend everything covered in this tour.
languageLesson: Vite resolve aliases like @/* to src/* must be mirrored in tsconfig paths so both the bundler and the typechecker resolve imports identically; otherwise builds succeed while typechecking fails.
title: Build and Tooling
